questions.q:
**Questions 1–6 | TRUE / FALSE / NOT GIVEN**

Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 1?

---

**Question 1.** There are other parrots that share the kakapo's inability to fly.
questions.passage:
**Test 1 – Reading Passage 1: The kākāpō**

The kākāpō is a nocturnal, flightless parrot that is critically endangered and one of New Zealand's unique treasures.

The kākāpō, also known as the owl parrot, is a large, forest-dwelling bird, with a pale owl-like face. Up to 64 cm in length, it has predominantly yellow-green feathers, forward-facing eyes, a large grey beak, large blue feet, and relatively short wings and tail. **It is the world's only flightless parrot**, and is also possibly one of the world's longest-living birds, with a reported lifespan of up to 100 years.

Kākāpō are solitary birds and tend to occupy the same home range for many years. They forage on the ground and climb high into trees. They often leap from trees and flap their wings, but at best manage a controlled descent to the ground. They are entirely vegetarian, with their diet including the leaves, roots and bark of trees as well as bulbs, and fern fronds.

Kākāpō breed in summer and autumn, **but only in years when food is plentiful**. **Males play no part in incubation or chick-rearing** – females alone incubate eggs and feed the chicks. The 1–4 eggs are laid in soil, which is repeatedly turned over before and during incubation.
questions.explanation:
**FALSE.** The passage explicitly states the kākāpō 'is the world's **only** flightless parrot', which directly contradicts the idea that other parrots share this trait.

> **Vocabulary note:** *flightless* /ˈflaɪtləs/ = unable to fly | *nocturnal* /nɒkˈtɜːnəl/ = active at night

questions.q: **Question 2.** Adult kakapo produce chicks every year.
questions.passage:
**Test 1 – Reading Passage 1: The kākāpō** *(continued)*

Kākāpō breed in summer and autumn, **but only in years when food is plentiful**. Males play no part in incubation or chick-rearing – females alone incubate eggs and feed the chicks.
questions.explanation:
**FALSE.** The passage states kākāpō breed 'only in years when food is plentiful' — not every year. Breeding is conditional on food availability.

> **Vocabulary note:** *plentiful* /ˈplentɪfəl/ = available in large amounts | *incubation* /ˌɪŋkjʊˈbeɪʃən/ = keeping eggs warm until they hatch

questions.q: **Question 3.** Adult male kakapo bring food back to nesting females.
questions.passage:
**Test 1 – Reading Passage 1: The kākāpō** *(continued)*

**Males play no part in incubation or chick-rearing** – females alone incubate eggs and feed the chicks. The female kākāpō has to spend long periods away from the nest searching for food.
questions.explanation:
**FALSE.** The passage is unambiguous: males 'play **no part** in incubation or chick-rearing'. Females alone both incubate eggs and find food.

> **Vocabulary note:** *chick-rearing* = raising young birds | *unattended* = without supervision or care

questions.q: **Question 4.** The Polynesian rat was a greater threat to the kakapo than Polynesian settlers.
questions.passage:
**Test 1 – Reading Passage 1: The kākāpō** *(continued)*

Before humans arrived, kākāpō were common throughout New Zealand's forests. With the arrival of the first Polynesian settlers about 700 years ago, the flightless kākāpō was easy prey. They ate its meat and used its feathers to make soft cloaks. **With them came the Polynesian dog and rat, which also preyed on kākāpō.**
questions.explanation:
**NOT GIVEN.** Both Polynesian settlers and their animals (dogs and rats) are mentioned as threats, but the passage never **compares** their relative impact. There is no information to judge which was the greater danger.

> **Key IELTS tip:** NOT GIVEN means the passage neither confirms nor contradicts the statement — there is simply no information on this comparison.

questions.q: **Question 5.** Kakapo were transferred from Rakiura Island to other locations because they were at risk from feral cats.
questions.passage:
**Test 1 – Reading Passage 1: The kākāpō** *(continued)*

Unfortunately, **predation by feral cats on Rakiura Island led to a rapid decline in kākāpō numbers**. As a result, during 1980–97, the surviving population was evacuated to three island sanctuaries: Codfish Island, Maud Island and Little Barrier Island.
questions.explanation:
**TRUE.** The passage directly states that 'predation by feral cats on Rakiura Island led to a rapid decline in kākāpō numbers', and this caused the evacuation ('As a result...').

> **Vocabulary note:** *feral* /ˈferəl/ = (of an animal) living in the wild, having escaped from captivity | *predation* /prɪˈdeɪʃən/ = the act of killing and eating prey

questions.q: **Question 6.** One Recovery Plan initiative that helped increase the kakapo population size was caring for struggling young birds.
questions.passage:
**Test 1 – Reading Passage 1: The kākāpō** *(continued)*

This [intensive management] involved moving the birds between islands, supplementary feeding of adults and **rescuing and hand-raising any failing chicks**.

After the first five years of the Recovery Plan, the population was on target. By 2000, five new females had been produced, and the total population had grown to 62 birds.
questions.explanation:
**TRUE.** 'Rescuing and hand-raising any failing chicks' directly corresponds to 'caring for struggling young birds'. The population subsequently grew, confirming this helped.

> **Paraphrase recognition (key IELTS skill):** *'failing chicks'* (passage) = *'struggling young birds'* (statement) | *'rescuing and hand-raising'* = *'caring for'*

questions.q: **Question 7.** The diet of the kākāpō consists of fern fronds, various parts of a tree and _______.
questions.passage:
**Test 1 – Reading Passage 1: The kākāpō** — Note Completion (Questions 7–13)

Choose **ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER** from the passage for each answer.

| New Zealand's kākāpō |
|---|
| **A type of parrot:** |
| · diet consists of fern fronds, various parts of a tree and **[Q7]** |
| · nests are created in **[Q8]** where eggs are laid |
| **Arrival of Polynesian settlers** |
| · the **[Q9]** of the kākāpō were used to make clothes |
| **Arrival of European colonisers** |
| · **[Q10]** were an animal which they introduced that ate the kākāpō's food sources |
| **Protecting kākāpō** |
| · a definite sighting of female kākāpō on Rakiura Island was reported in the year **[Q11]** |
| · the Recovery Plan included an increase in **[Q12]** |
| · a current goal of the Recovery Plan is to maintain the involvement of **[Q13]** in kākāpō protection |

---
*Passage reference:* 'They are entirely vegetarian, with their diet including the leaves, roots and bark of trees as well as **bulbs**, and fern fronds.'
questions.explanation:
**BULBS.** The passage lists 'leaves, roots and bark of trees as well as **bulbs**, and fern fronds'. The note already accounts for 'fern fronds' and 'various parts of a tree' (leaves/roots/bark), leaving **bulbs** as the missing item.

> **Vocabulary note:** *bulbs* /bʌlbz/ = rounded underground plant storage organs (e.g., onion bulbs) | *fronds* /frɒndz/ = leaf-like parts of ferns

questions.q: **Question 8.** Nests are created in _______ where eggs are laid.
questions.passage:
**Test 1 – Reading Passage 1** *(note completion continued)*

*Passage reference:* 'The 1–4 eggs are laid in **soil**, which is repeatedly turned over before and during incubation.'
questions.explanation:
**SOIL.** The passage states 'The 1–4 eggs are laid in **soil**, which is repeatedly turned over.' The kākāpō lays eggs directly in the soil, not in a constructed nest above ground.

> **Vocabulary note:** *incubation* /ˌɪŋkjʊˈbeɪʃən/ = the process of keeping eggs warm until they hatch

questions.q: **Question 9.** The _______ of the kākāpō were used to make clothes.
questions.passage:
**Test 1 – Reading Passage 1** *(note completion continued)*

*Passage reference:* 'They ate its meat and used its **feathers** to make soft cloaks.'
questions.explanation:
**FEATHERS.** The passage states Polynesian settlers 'used its **feathers** to make soft cloaks'. Cloaks are a type of clothing, matching 'clothes' in the note.

> **Paraphrase:** *'cloaks'* (passage) = *'clothes'* (note) | *feathers* /ˈfeðəz/ = the light, flat structures that cover a bird's body

questions.q: **Question 10.** _______ were an animal which European colonisers introduced that ate the kākāpō's food sources.
questions.passage:
**Test 1 – Reading Passage 1** *(note completion continued)*

*Passage reference:* 'A great deal of habitat was lost through forest clearance, and introduced species such as **deer** depleted the remaining forests of food.'
questions.explanation:
**DEER.** The passage states 'introduced species such as **deer** depleted the remaining forests of food.' Deer consumed the vegetation the kākāpō relied upon. (Cats and stoats were predators, not food competitors.)

> **Vocabulary note:** *depleted* /dɪˈpliːtɪd/ = reduced greatly in quantity | *habitat* /ˈhæbɪtæt/ = the natural environment where an animal lives

questions.q: **Question 11.** A definite sighting of female kākāpō on Rakiura Island was reported in the year _______.
questions.passage:
**Test 1 – Reading Passage 1** *(note completion continued)*

*Passage reference:* 'In 1977, a large population of males was spotted in Rakiura... There were about 200 individuals, and **in 1980 it was confirmed females were also present**.'
questions.explanation:
**1980.** Although males were spotted in 1977, it was **1980** when 'it was confirmed females were also present' on Rakiura Island. 1974 relates to a new search initiative; 1996 is when the Recovery Plan was launched.

> **Distractor awareness:** 1977 is when the large male population was spotted — not when females were confirmed.

questions.q: **Question 12.** The Recovery Plan included an increase in _______.
questions.passage:
**Test 1 – Reading Passage 1** *(note completion continued)*

*Passage reference:* 'In 1996, a new Recovery Plan was launched, together with a specialist advisory group... and a higher amount of **funding**.'
questions.explanation:
**FUNDING.** The passage states the 1996 Recovery Plan came with 'a higher amount of **funding**', directly matching the note's gap.

> **Vocabulary note:** *funding* /ˈfʌndɪŋ/ = money provided for a specific purpose | *advisory committee* = a group formed to give expert advice

questions.q: **Question 13.** A current goal of the Recovery Plan is to maintain the involvement of _______ in kākāpō protection.
questions.passage:
**Test 1 – Reading Passage 1** *(note completion continued)*

*Passage reference:* 'Its key goals are: minimise the loss of genetic diversity... restore or maintain sufficient habitat... and ensure **stakeholders** continue to be fully engaged in the preservation of the species.'
questions.explanation:
**STAKEHOLDERS.** The passage lists 'ensure **stakeholders** continue to be fully engaged in the preservation of the species' as a key current goal.

> **Vocabulary note:** *stakeholders* /ˈsteɪkˌhəʊldəz/ = people or groups with an interest or concern in something | *genetic diversity* = variety in the DNA of a population

questions.q:
**Questions 14–18 | Section Matching**

Reading Passage 2 has seven sections, **A–G**. Which section contains the following information?

---

**Question 14.** Reference to the research problems that arise from there being only a few surviving large elms.
questions.passage:
**Test 1 – Reading Passage 2: Elms returning to Britain**

**A** Around 25 million elms, accounting for 90% of all elm trees in the UK, died during the 1960s and '70s of Dutch elm disease. However, there's now hope the elm may be reintroduced to the countryside of central and southern England.

**B** The disease is caused by a fungus that blocks the elms' vascular (water, nutrient and food transport) system. A first epidemic occurred in the 1920s... a second epidemic was **triggered by shipments of elm from Canada**. The wood came in the form of logs destined for boat building and its intact bark was perfect for the elm bark beetles that spread the deadly fungus.

**C** Today, elms still exist in the southern English countryside but mostly only in low hedgerows... Once the trunk of the elm reaches **10–15 centimetres or so in diameter**, it becomes a perfect size for beetles to lay eggs and for the fungus to take hold. Yet mature specimens have been identified... **opportunities are limited as the number of these mature survivors is relatively small.** 'I don't see how it can be entirely down to luck,' says Russell.

**D** For centuries, elm ran a close second to oak as the hardwood tree of choice in Britain...

**E** Today, the city of Brighton's elms total about 17,000. **Strong winds from the sea make it difficult for the determined elm bark beetle to attack this coastal city's elm population.** However, the situation is precarious. 'The beetles can just march in if we're not careful, as the threat is right on our doorstep,' says Bourne.

**F** A new generation of seedlings have been bred and tested... 'The effects are very quick,' says Russell. 'You return in four to six weeks and trees that are resistant show no symptoms...'

**G** All of this raises questions of social acceptance... For her, the environmental case for reintroducing elm is strong... **Others are more wary.** 'You're replacing a native species with a horticultural analogue. You're effectively cloning,' says Elliot. There's also the risk of introducing new diseases.
questions.explanation:
**Section C.** It states 'opportunities are limited as the number of these mature survivors is relatively small' — directly identifying the research problem caused by the scarcity of surviving large elms.

> **Key phrase:** *'relatively small'* signals a limiting research condition.

questions.q: **Question 15.** Details of a difference of opinion about the value of reintroducing elms to Britain.
questions.passage: **Test 1 – Reading Passage 2** *(refer to full passage above)*
questions.explanation:
**Section G.** Russell believes 'the environmental case for reintroducing elm is strong', while Elliot warns you'd be 'replacing a native species with a horticultural analogue' and risks introducing new diseases. These are two contrasting expert opinions.

> **Vocabulary note:** *horticultural analogue* = a cultivated plant species genetically similar to an existing native species

questions.q: **Question 16.** Reference to how Dutch elm disease was brought into Britain.
questions.passage: **Test 1 – Reading Passage 2** *(refer to full passage above)*
questions.explanation:
**Section B.** It explains that 'a second epidemic was triggered by **shipments of elm from Canada**. The wood came in the form of logs destined for boat building and its intact bark was perfect for the elm bark beetles that spread the deadly fungus.'

> **Vocabulary note:** *virulent* /ˈvɪrʊlənt/ = extremely severe or harmful | *vascular system* = the internal transport network of a plant

questions.q: **Question 17.** A description of the conditions that have enabled a location in Britain to escape Dutch elm disease.
questions.passage: **Test 1 – Reading Passage 2** *(refer to full passage above)*
questions.explanation:
**Section E.** Brighton is described as having survived: 'Strong winds from the sea make it difficult for the determined elm bark beetle to attack this coastal city's elm population.' This is the specific local condition enabling escape from the disease.

> **Vocabulary note:** *precarious* /prɪˈkeərɪəs/ = not safe or secure; likely to change suddenly

questions.q: **Question 18.** Reference to the stage at which young elms become vulnerable to Dutch elm disease.
questions.passage: **Test 1 – Reading Passage 2** *(refer to full passage above)*
questions.explanation:
**Section C.** It states: 'Once the trunk of the elm reaches **10–15 centimetres** or so in diameter, it becomes a perfect size for beetles to lay eggs and for the fungus to take hold.' This specifies the developmental stage of vulnerability.

> **Note:** Section C correctly answers both Q14 and Q18 — the instruction states letters may be used more than once.

questions.passage:
**Test 1 – Reading Passage 2: Matching Statements to People (Questions 19–23)**

Match each statement with the correct person. You may use any letter more than once.

| Person | Role | Key Quotes |
|---|---|---|
| **A. Matt Elliot** | Woodland Trust | 'You look at old photographs from the 1960s and it's only then that you realise the impact [elms had]... They were significant, large trees … then they were gone.' / 'Sometimes the best thing you can do is just give nature time to recover ... over time, you might get resistance.' |
| **B. Karen Russell** | Co-author, *'Where we are with elm'* | 'We have millions of small elms in hedgerows but they get targeted by the beetle as soon as they reach a certain size.' / 'The effects are very quick... I don't see how it can be entirely down to luck.' |
| **C. Peter Bourne** | National Elm Collection, Brighton | 'I saw Dutch elm disease unfold as a small boy...' / 'The beetles can just march in if we're not careful, as the threat is right on our doorstep.' |

---

**Question 19.** *'If a tree gets infected with Dutch elm disease, the damage rapidly becomes visible.'*
questions.explanation:
**B – Karen Russell.** She states: 'The effects are very quick. You return in four to six weeks and trees that are susceptible show leaf loss and may even have died completely.' The rapid visibility of damage is her key observation.

> **Paraphrase:** *'effects are very quick'* = *'damage rapidly becomes visible'*

questions.q: **Question 20.** *'It may be better to wait and see if the mature elms that have survived continue to flourish.'*
questions.passage: **Test 1 – Reading Passage 2** *(refer to people list above)*
questions.explanation:
**A – Matt Elliot.** He says: 'Sometimes the best thing you can do is just give nature **time to recover** ... over time, you might get resistance.' This reflects a cautious 'wait and observe' approach to surviving elms.

> **Vocabulary note:** *flourish* /ˈflʌrɪʃ/ = grow or develop in a healthy way | *resistance* = the ability to withstand disease

questions.q: **Question 21.** *'There must be an explanation for the survival of some mature elms.'*
questions.passage: **Test 1 – Reading Passage 2** *(refer to people list above)*
questions.explanation:
**B – Karen Russell.** She asks: 'What are the reasons for their survival? Avoidance, tolerance, resistance? We don't know where the balance lies between the three. **I don't see how it can be entirely down to luck.**' — implying a non-random, explicable cause.

> **Key inference:** Saying it cannot be 'entirely down to luck' implies a logical explanation must exist.

questions.q: **Question 22.** *'We need to be aware that insects carrying Dutch elm disease are not very far away.'*
questions.passage: **Test 1 – Reading Passage 2** *(refer to people list above)*
questions.explanation:
**C – Peter Bourne.** He warns: 'The beetles can just march in if we're not careful, as **the threat is right on our doorstep**.' 'On our doorstep' is a colloquial expression meaning very nearby.

> **Collocation:** *'on our doorstep'* = very close by | *'march in'* = advance steadily and relentlessly

questions.q: **Question 23.** *'You understand the effect Dutch elm disease has had when you see evidence of how prominent the tree once was.'*
questions.passage: **Test 1 – Reading Passage 2** *(refer to people list above)*
questions.explanation:
**A – Matt Elliot.** He says: 'You look at **old photographs** from the 1960s and it's **only then** that you realise the impact [elms had]... They were significant, large trees … then they were gone.' Old photographs serve as evidence of the tree's former prominence.

> **Paraphrase:** *'old photographs'* = *'evidence of how prominent the tree once was'*

questions.q: **Question 24.** For hundreds of years, the only tree more popular in Britain than elm was _______.
questions.passage:
**Test 1 – Reading Passage 2: Summary Completion (Questions 24–26)**

Complete the summary below. Choose **ONE WORD ONLY** from the passage for each answer.

---

**Uses of a popular tree**

*For hundreds of years, the only tree that was more popular in Britain than elm was* **[Q24]**. *Starting in the Bronze Age, many tools were made from elm and people also used it to make weapons. In the 18th century, it was grown to provide wood for boxes and* **[Q25]**. *Due to its strength, elm was often used for mining equipment and the Cutty Sark's* **[Q26]** *was also constructed from elm.*

---
*Passage reference (Section D):* 'For centuries, elm ran a close second to **oak** as the hardwood tree of choice in Britain... In the 18th century, it was planted more widely and its wood was used for items such as storage crates and **flooring**... used to build the **keel** of the 19th-century sailing ship Cutty Sark as well as mining equipment.'
questions.explanation:
**OAK.** The passage states 'elm ran a close second to **oak** as the hardwood tree of choice in Britain', meaning oak was the only tree more popular.

> **Vocabulary note:** *hardwood* = dense wood from deciduous trees, used in construction and furniture | Common hardwoods: oak /əʊk/, elm /elm/, ash /æʃ/, birch /bɜːtʃ/

questions.q: **Question 25.** In the 18th century, elm was grown to provide wood for boxes and _______.
questions.passage:
**Test 1 – Reading Passage 2** *(summary continued)*

*Passage reference:* 'In the 18th century, it was planted more widely and its wood was used for items such as storage crates and **flooring**.'
questions.explanation:
**FLOORING.** The passage mentions 'storage crates and **flooring**'. In the summary, 'boxes' paraphrases 'storage crates', so the missing word is **flooring**.

> **Paraphrase:** *'storage crates'* = *'boxes'* | *flooring* /ˈflɔːrɪŋ/ = material used to make floors

questions.q: **Question 26.** The Cutty Sark's _______ was also constructed from elm.
questions.passage:
**Test 1 – Reading Passage 2** *(summary continued)*

*Passage reference:* 'It was... used to build the **keel** of the 19th-century sailing ship Cutty Sark as well as mining equipment.'
questions.explanation:
**KEEL.** The passage specifically names 'the **keel** of the 19th-century sailing ship Cutty Sark'. The keel is the main structural beam running along the bottom of a ship.

> **Vocabulary note:** *keel* /kiːl/ = the central structural beam at the bottom of a ship's hull | The Cutty Sark is a famous 19th-century British clipper ship.

questions.q:
**Questions 27–30 | Multiple Choice**

Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

---

**Question 27.** In the first paragraph, the writer introduces the topic of the text by:

A. defining some commonly used terms.
B. questioning a widely held assumption.
C. mentioning a challenge faced by everyone.
D. specifying a situation which makes us most anxious.
questions.passage:
**Test 1 – Reading Passage 3: How stress affects our judgement**

*Paragraph 1:* 'Some of the most important decisions of our lives occur while we're feeling stressed and anxious. From medical decisions to financial and professional ones, **we are all sometimes required to weigh up information under stressful conditions**. But do we become better or worse at processing and using information under such circumstances?'

*Paragraph 2:* 'My colleague and I, both neuroscientists, wanted to investigate how the mind operates under stress, so we visited some local fire stations. **Firefighters' workdays vary quite a bit.** Some are pretty relaxed... Other days can be hectic, with numerous life-threatening incidents to attend to... **These ups and downs presented the perfect setting for an experiment** on how people's ability to use information changes when they feel under pressure.'

*Paragraph 3:* 'We found that perceived threat acted as a trigger for a stress reaction that made the task of processing information easier for the firefighters – but only as long as it conveyed bad news.'

*Paragraph 4:* '**This is how we arrived at these results.** We asked the firefighters to estimate their likelihood of experiencing 40 different adverse events... We then gave them either good news... or bad news... and asked them to provide new estimates.'

*Paragraph 5:* 'People are normally quite optimistic – they will ignore bad news and embrace the good. **This is what happened when the firefighters were relaxed**; but when they were under stress, a different pattern emerged. Under these conditions, they became hyper-vigilant to bad news... and altered their beliefs in response. In contrast, **stress didn't change how they responded to good news.**'

*Paragraph 7:* '**Brain imaging reveals that this 'switch' is related to a sudden boost in a neural signal important for learning, specifically in response to unexpected warning signs, such as faces expressing fear.**'
questions.explanation:
**C.** The writer states 'we **are all** sometimes required to weigh up information under stressful conditions' — stress-based decision-making is presented as a **universal** challenge. No terms are defined (not A); no assumption is questioned (not B); the paragraph does not identify the *most* anxiety-inducing situation (not D).

> **Exam strategy:** Eliminate options by checking each against the exact wording of the paragraph.
options: A – defining some commonly used terms
B – questioning a widely held assumption
C – mentioning a challenge faced by everyone
D – specifying a situation which makes us most anxious

questions.q:
**Question 28.** What point does the writer make about firefighters in the second paragraph?

A. The regular changes of stress levels in their working lives make them ideal study subjects.
B. The strategies they use to handle stress are of particular interest to researchers.
C. The stressful nature of their job is typical of many public service professions.
D. Their personalities make them especially well-suited to working under stress.
questions.passage: **Test 1 – Reading Passage 3** *(refer to passage above)*
questions.explanation:
**A.** The passage says firefighters' varying workdays — from relaxed to extremely high-pressure — 'presented the **perfect setting** for an experiment'. It is the **variation** in stress levels (not personalities or strategies) that makes them suitable subjects.

> **Paraphrase:** *'ups and downs'* + *'perfect setting for an experiment'* = *'ideal study subjects due to regular changes in stress levels'*
options: A – Regular stress-level variation makes them ideal study subjects
B – Their stress-handling strategies interest researchers
C – Their stressful job is typical of public service professions
D – Their personalities suit them to stress

questions.q:
**Question 29.** What is the writer doing in the fourth paragraph?

A. Explaining their findings.
B. Justifying their approach.
C. Setting out their objectives.
D. Describing their methodology.
questions.passage: **Test 1 – Reading Passage 3** *(refer to passage above)*
questions.explanation:
**D.** The paragraph begins with 'This is **how** we arrived at these results' and then details the step-by-step procedure: what participants were asked, what stimuli were given, and what was measured. This is the **methodology** (method/procedure section).

> **Academic writing note:** *Methodology* describes **how** research was conducted. *Findings* describe **what** was discovered. The paragraph uses procedural language: 'We asked...', 'We gave...', 'We asked them to provide...'

questions.q:
**Question 30.** In the seventh paragraph, the writer describes a mechanism in the brain which:

A. Enables people to respond more quickly to stressful situations.
B. Results in increased ability to control our levels of anxiety.
C. Produces heightened sensitivity to indications of external threats.
D. Is activated when there is a need to communicate a sense of danger.
questions.passage:
**Test 1 – Reading Passage 3** *(continued)*

*Paragraph 7:* 'When we experience stressful events, a physiological change is triggered that causes us to take in warnings and focus on what might go wrong. **Brain imaging reveals that this 'switch' is related to a sudden boost in a neural signal important for learning, specifically in response to unexpected warning signs, such as faces expressing fear.**'
questions.explanation:
**C.** The 'neural signal' boosts our response 'specifically in response to **unexpected warning signs**' (external threats). This constitutes **heightened sensitivity to indications of external threats**. The passage does not mention speed (not A), anxiety control (not B), or communicating danger to others (not D).

> **Vocabulary note:** *neural* /ˈnjʊərəl/ = relating to a nerve or the nervous system | *physiological* /ˌfɪzɪəˈlɒdʒɪkəl/ = relating to the physical functions of the body
options: A – Enables faster responses to stressful situations
B – Increases ability to control anxiety
C – Produces heightened sensitivity to external threat signals

questions.q:
**Question 31.** Complete the sentence:

'At times when they were relaxed, the firefighters usually ___'
questions.passage:
**Test 1 – Reading Passage 3: Sentence Completion (Questions 31–35)**

Complete each sentence with the correct ending **A–G** below.

**Sentence stems:**
- 31. At times when they were relaxed, the firefighters usually ___
- 32. The researchers noted that when the firefighters were stressed, they ___
- 33. When the firefighters were told good news, they always ___
- 34. The students' cortisol levels and heart rates were affected when the researchers ___
- 35. In both experiments, negative information was processed better when the subjects ___

**Endings:**

| | |
|---|---|
| **A** | made them feel optimistic. |
| **B** | took relatively little notice of bad news. |
| **C** | responded to negative and positive information in the same way. |
| **D** | were feeling under stress. |
| **E** | put them in a stressful situation. |
| **F** | behaved in a similar manner, regardless of the circumstances. |
| **G** | thought it more likely that they would experience something bad. |

---
*Key passage evidence:*
- *'People are normally quite optimistic – they will ignore bad news and embrace the good. **This is what happened when the firefighters were relaxed.**'*
- *'Under [stress]... they became **hyper-vigilant to bad news**... and altered their beliefs in response.'*
- *'stress didn't change how they responded to **good news**'*
- *'students who were told they had to give a surprise public speech... their **cortisol levels spiked**, their **heart rates went up**'*
questions.explanation:

questions.q: **Question 36.** The tone of the content we post on social media tends to reflect the nature of the posts in our feeds.
questions.passage:
**Test 1 – Reading Passage 3: How stress affects our judgement** *(Questions 36–40)*

Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 3?

Write **YES / NO / NOT GIVEN**.

---
*Relevant passage excerpts:*

- *'Studies show that if we observe positive feeds on social media... we are more likely to post uplifting messages ourselves. If we observe negative posts... we will in turn create more negative posts.'* [→ Q36]

- *'Repeatedly checking your phone, according to a survey conducted by the American Psychological Association, is related to stress.'* [→ Q37]

- *'...stress is triggered, spreading from one person to the next, which temporarily **enhances** the likelihood that people will **take in** negative reports...'* [→ Q38]

- *'trips are cancelled, even if the disaster took place across the globe; stocks are sold, even when holding on is the best thing to do.'* [→ Q39]

- *'The good news, however, is that positive emotions, such as hope, are contagious too, and are powerful in inducing people to act to find solutions.'* [→ Q40]
questions.explanation:
**YES.** The passage directly supports this: positive feeds → uplifting posts; negative feeds → negative posts. Our output mirrors our input.

> **Vocabulary note:** *contagious* /kənˈteɪdʒəs/ = spreading rapidly from person to person | *feeds* = the stream of posts shown on a social media platform

questions.q: **Question 37.** Phones have a greater impact on our stress levels than other electronic media devices.
questions.passage: **Test 1 – Reading Passage 3** *(refer to passage above)*
questions.explanation:
**NOT GIVEN.** The passage mentions that 'repeatedly checking your phone is related to stress', but makes **no comparison** between phones and other electronic devices (tablets, computers, televisions, etc.). There is insufficient information to judge the claim.

> **IELTS tip:** NOT GIVEN ≠ FALSE. The statement is not contradicted — it simply cannot be verified from the text.

questions.q: **Question 38.** The more we read about a stressful public event on social media, the less able we are to take the information in.
questions.passage: **Test 1 – Reading Passage 3** *(refer to passage above)*
questions.explanation:
**NO.** This contradicts the passage. Stress actually **increases** our ability to absorb negative information: it 'temporarily **enhances** the likelihood that people will **take in** negative reports.' More exposure to alarming news leads to *greater* uptake, not less.

> **Contrast:** Statement says *'less able to take in'* ↔ Passage says stress *'enhances the likelihood of taking in negative reports'*

questions.q: **Question 39.** Stress created by social media posts can lead us to take unnecessary precautions.
questions.passage: **Test 1 – Reading Passage 3** *(refer to passage above)*
questions.explanation:
**YES.** The passage gives concrete examples of unnecessary actions triggered by media-spread stress: 'trips are cancelled, **even if** the disaster took place across the globe; stocks are sold, **even when holding on is the best thing to do**.' These are precautions that are unnecessary given the actual risk level.

> **Vocabulary note:** *precautions* /prɪˈkɔːʃənz/ = actions taken in advance to prevent something bad | *collective fear* = anxiety shared widely across a group or society

questions.q: **Question 40.** Our tendency to be affected by other people's moods can be used in a positive way.
questions.passage: **Test 1 – Reading Passage 3** *(refer to passage above)*
questions.explanation:
**YES.** The passage concludes: 'positive emotions, such as hope, are contagious too, and are powerful in inducing people to **act to find solutions**. Being aware of the close relationship between people's emotional state and how they process information can help us **frame our messages more effectively** and become **conscientious agents of change**.' This confirms mood contagion can be harnessed positively.

> **Vocabulary note:** *conscientious* /ˌkɒnʃɪˈenʃəs/ = showing careful attention and effort | *agents of change* = people who actively drive positive transformation
